title: US Chip Curbs and Distillation Crackdown Slow China's AI Model Race
excerpt: Z.AI's GLM-5.5 flagship has slipped behind schedule and Moonshot expects its release cycle could double if overseas computing access is cut, Reuters reports, as a November 19 US rule targets Chinese firms' use of advanced chips in overseas data centres.
body:
• China's Z.AI has fallen behind schedule on GLM-5.5, its next flagship AI model, partly because of increasingly effective safeguards against distillation, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
  • A US Commerce Department rule that took effect on November 19 restricts Chinese companies' access to large amounts of computing power from advanced US chips in overseas data centres.
  • Moonshot AI expects the interval between its major model releases could double, from six months to a year or longer, if it loses access to overseas computing power.
  • Anthropic said in September it had observed nearly 200 million exchanges with its Claude models linked to suspected distillation campaigns, attributing them to Chinese developers including Alibaba, Moonshot and Z.AI.

New US chip restrictions and a crackdown on distillation are slowing the development of China's leading artificial intelligence models, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Z.AI has fallen behind schedule on its next flagship model, while rival Moonshot AI expects the gap between its major releases could double if it loses access to overseas computing power.

The measures threaten a key advantage that has helped Chinese AI companies challenge their American rivals despite years of export controls: the ability to develop competitive models at substantially lower cost.

The new chip rule

A US Commerce Department rule that took effect on November 19 imposes licensing requirements aimed at restricting Chinese companies' access to large amounts of computing power from advanced US chips in overseas data centres. The rule targets a route by which Chinese developers could use Nvidia processors without importing them into China.

Moonshot is particularly exposed because it rents computing power to train its models and prioritises overseas providers, according to a person with knowledge of its operations. The Beijing-based developer internally expects its usual six-month interval between major releases could stretch to 12 months or longer if that access is cut off entirely, and the person estimated its next flagship model, Kimi K4, could be delayed until around the middle of 2027. Moonshot released Kimi K2 in July 2025, K2.5 in January and K3 in July.

Z.AI's delayed flagship

Z.AI, also known as Zhipu AI, had planned to release its next flagship model, GLM-5.5, this month but has yet to do so, two people familiar with the matter said. The model, designed with roughly 3 trillion parameters, has been held up partly by increasingly effective safeguards against distillation, one of the people said. Z.AI had hoped to complete training and release the model by year-end, but the new US computing restrictions could push its launch into the first quarter of 2027 or later.

On Monday, the company instead released GLM-5.4, built on an existing model with 750 billion parameters; Z.AI says a new design enables it to match the performance of models with 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameters.

The distillation fight

Distillation is a technique in which developers train a model using answers generated by a more capable one. US companies have moved to block its unauthorised use: Anthropic said in September it had observed nearly 200 million exchanges with its Claude models linked to suspected distillation campaigns, attributing them to Chinese developers including Alibaba, Moonshot and Z.AI, and OpenAI has also reported efforts to disrupt such activity.

Moonshot did not respond immediately to a request for comment; it has previously rejected suggestions that its Kimi K3 model's performance was achieved via distillation, telling China's National Business Daily in July that its gains came from original changes to its underlying architecture. Z.AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

What to watch

The next markers are whether Z.AI can complete GLM-5.5 training by year-end as it had hoped, and how the November 19 licensing rule is applied to overseas data-centre capacity in practice. For now, the people Reuters spoke to describe longer development cycles, not a halt: Chinese labs are still releasing models, but the low-cost path that let them close the gap with US rivals is getting narrower.
